subject: PSHE
board: PSHE Association / statutory Relationships and Health Education guidance
source: National Curriculum / statutory guidance (Relationships Education and Health Education only); PSHE Association programme of study themes; TGA RSHE Policy 2026-27 and TGA RECIPE Character Framework 2026-27 (Drive); existing TGA PSHE Y1-Y2 lesson style. Qur'an and hadith references limited to well-known authenticated sources and cited plainly. No RSE or sex education in Years 1 to 6 (owner decision, October 2026): body-safety safeguarding only, taught at a non-sexual level.

lessons.title: Being a good friend: kind words and kind actions
objectives: Describe what makes a good friend
Use kind words and avoid unkind nicknames
Link kindness to our RECIPE values

keywords.def: someone you trust, enjoy and care for
being gentle, helpful and caring
a name used instead of someone's real name
good manners and behaviour
to make sure everyone can join in

starter: Name one way to be kind in a live lesson.
Who is a trusted adult you can go to?

teach.heading: What makes a good friend?
teach.note: Say bismillah. Recap the RECIPE values from earlier years (Resilience, Eeman, Contentment, Integrity, Progress, Excellence). Today links to Integrity and Excellence in how we treat others. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day. Ask: ‘What do you like about your best friend?’ Take answers without names if pupils prefer.

teach.heading: Kind words
bullets: Say please, thank you and sorry
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that a smile is charity (Tirmidhi). Model giving a sincere compliment to a pupil's work. Ask: ‘How do you feel when someone is kind to you?’ Misconception: kindness is only for friends. It is for everyone.

teach.heading: Names we use
bullets: Qur'an 49:11: do not call each other bad names
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 49:11 tells believers not to mock one another or call each other offensive nicknames. Distinguish a kind family nickname that the person loves from a name that makes someone feel small. Ask: ‘How can we check?’ (ask them; stop if they dislike it).

teach.heading: Including everyone
bullets: Be a friend to new classmates
teach.note: Role-play: someone new joins the group in a break-out room or class game. Ask: ‘What can you say?’ Model: ‘Would you like to join us?’ Link to the hadith that none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself (Bukhari and Muslim). Keep language simple for Year 3.

practice: Sort into kind or unkind: (a) ‘You can’t play.’ (b) ‘Would you like to join?’ (c) Laughing at someone’s mistake. (d) Sharing your pencil.
What could you say to a new child in class?
Rewrite this to be kinder: ‘Move, slowcoach!’
independent: Draw or write a ‘kind friend’ poster with five qualities and one example of a kind sentence.
Role-play with a partner: inviting someone to join a game, using polite words.
Write three kind compliments you could say to classmates.
exit: Name two ways to be a good friend.
Why should we avoid unkind nicknames?
lessons.homework: Do one kind act for someone at home and write one sentence about how it made them feel.
lessons.send: SEND: use picture cards for kind and unkind actions. EAL: key phrases in simple English with visuals. Stretch: write a short story where a child includes a lonely friend.

lessons.title: When friends fall out: solving problems and spotting bullying
objectives: Use steps to solve a disagreement kindly
Explain the difference between falling out and bullying
Know who to tell if bullying happens

keywords.def: when people do not agree
to say sorry and mean it
hurting someone on purpose, again and again
someone who helps when they see unkindness
a grown-up who helps keep you safe

starter: Give one kind word you can say to a friend.
Why should we use real names?

teach.heading: Disagreements happen
bullets: It is normal to feel cross
Anger is a feeling, not a rule
teach.note: Say bismillah. Normalise disagreements: all friends have them. Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said the strong person is the one who controls himself when angry (Bukhari and Muslim). Ask: ‘What does your body feel like when you are cross?’ Take answers: hot face, fast heart. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Steps to sort it out
bullets: Say how you feel: ‘I felt sad when…’
Find a fair answer and say sorry
teach.note: Model the steps with a scenario: two friends both want the same football turn. Show how to use ‘I’ statements rather than blame. Ask pupils to rehearse: ‘I felt left out when you ran off.’ Misconception: saying sorry fixes everything. We also need to change what we do.

teach.heading: Falling out or bullying?
bullets: Falling out: once, equal, both upset
Bullying can be words, hitting, leaving out, or online
Bullying is never the victim's fault
teach.note: Draw a two-column table on the board. Ask pupils to place examples. Emphasise that bullying involves power: one person or group keeps hurting another who finds it hard to stop it. Check understanding with thumbs up or down. Keep examples invented, not real pupils.

teach.heading: What can we do?
bullets: Walk away and tell a trusted adult
Help the person who is hurt
teach.note: Teach being an upstander: kindly support the targeted child and tell an adult. Reassure pupils that telling is not ‘snitching’, it is keeping people safe. Name trusted adults at home and in school. If a pupil discloses bullying, record and pass to the DSL or class teacher according to the Anti-Bullying and Safeguarding policies.

practice: Is it falling out or bullying? (a) Two friends argue once about a game. (b) A child is left out every break time on purpose. (c) A child keeps sending unkind messages in a game chat.
Put the steps in order: say sorry / stop and breathe / listen / say how you feel.
Who are three trusted adults you could tell?
independent: Write or act out a short conversation where two friends solve a disagreement using the steps.
Make a ‘What to do if I see bullying’ card with three actions.
Write one ‘I felt… when…’ sentence for an invented problem.
exit: What is the difference between falling out and bullying?
Name one thing you can do if you are being bullied.
lessons.homework: Tell a trusted adult at home one of the steps for solving a problem kindly and ask them to share a time they solved a disagreement.
lessons.send: SEND: provide visual steps cards. EAL: key phrases ‘Stop’, ‘Tell’, ‘Sorry’ with pictures. Stretch: write advice for a younger child about handling a falling out.

lessons.title: Staying safe online: sharing, strangers and telling someone
objectives: Explain what personal information is and why we protect it
Know what to do if something online feels wrong

keywords.def: facts that can identify you, such as your name, address or school
not to be shared with everyone
someone you do not know
to stop someone contacting you
to tell a grown-up or the app that something is wrong

starter: What should you do if someone is unkind to you?

teach.heading: Fun and safe online
bullets: Games, videos and lessons are useful
The internet has rules for safety
Ask a grown-up before you click
teach.note: Say bismillah. Begin by validating pupils' enjoyment of online games and videos. Explain that safe use means rules and trusted adults. Mention age limits: many apps are for ages 13 and over, and games have age ratings (PEGI). Misconception: a rule is there because adults want to spoil fun. It is there to protect. Ask: ‘What rules do you follow at home?’ Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Private information
bullets: Do not share your full name
Do not share your address or school
Do not share passwords or photos
Only trusted adults can help share
teach.note: Use a ‘secret box’ visual: private items go in; public ones are okay. Sort examples: favourite colour (okay), home address (private), school uniform photo (private). Passwords are like a key; only share with a parent or carer. Ask pupils to say what could go wrong if a stranger knew their address.

teach.heading: People online are not always who they say
bullets: Anyone can pretend to be a child
Do not meet someone you met online
teach.note: Explain calmly that some people online pretend to be someone else. Avoid frightening details. Teach the rule: if someone you do not know contacts you, do not reply, tell a grown-up. Ask: ‘Who would you tell?’ Reinforce that pupils are never in trouble for telling.

teach.heading: Stop, Block, Tell
bullets: Block: stop the person or account
Keep the evidence: do not delete
teach.note: Practise the words together. Reassure pupils that they will not lose their device for reporting. For worrying content or contact, they or a parent can use CEOP Safety Centre at ceop.police.uk. Remind pupils of Childline on 0800 1111 as a free, confidential helpline. Share tips with parents in the follow-up message.

practice: Sort into private or okay to share: (a) your favourite colour (b) your address (c) your password (d) your pet's name.
A stranger messages you in a game chat: ‘What school do you go to?’ What do you do?
Put in order: Tell / Stop / Block.
independent: Make a mini poster: ‘Stop, Block, Tell’ with one picture for each step.
Write three rules for staying safe online.
Role-play telling a trusted adult about an unkind message.
exit: Give two examples of personal information we should not share.
What are the three steps if something online feels wrong?
lessons.homework: Teach your family the ‘Stop, Block, Tell’ rule and ask them to help you make a family online safety rule.
lessons.send: SEND: use symbol cards and a sorting game. EAL: key vocabulary ‘private’, ‘stranger’, ‘block’. Stretch: write advice for a younger child about being safe in game chats.

lessons.title: Healthy habits: food, sleep, movement and screen balance
objectives: Name habits that keep our bodies healthy
Explain why sleep, food and exercise matter
Make a plan for balanced screen time

keywords.def: good for your body and mind
giving the right amount of time to different things
rest your body needs each night
movement that keeps your body strong
time spent using a phone, tablet, TV or computer

starter: Name one rule for being safe online.
What are the three steps if something feels wrong online?
Give an example of private information.

teach.heading: A healthy body is an amanah
bullets: Our bodies are a trust from Allah
Prophet (peace be upon him): your body has a right over you
teach.note: Say bismillah. Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that your body has a right over you (Bukhari). Ask: ‘What does it mean to look after something you have been given?’ Take answers. Keep language gentle; avoid body shaming; foods are not ‘good’ or ‘bad’, but some are for everyday and some for sometimes. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Eating well
bullets: Eat slowly and stop when comfortably full
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught one-third food, one-third drink and one-third for air (Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah). Show a simple plate with half vegetables and fruit, a quarter starchy food, a quarter protein. Be sensitive to families' circumstances and food choices. Ask: ‘What is one food that gives you energy?’

teach.heading: Sleep and movement
bullets: Children need about 9-11 hours of sleep
Good sleep helps learning and mood
Move for at least 60 minutes a day
teach.note: Explain that sleep helps the brain remember and the body grow. Suggest a bedtime routine: wash, dua, book, lights out. The 60 minutes of daily activity is NHS guidance for children. Ask: ‘How do you feel after a good night's sleep?’ Link to adab of sleeping and waking.

teach.heading: Balancing screen time
bullets: Screens are fun but can take over
Make time for family, prayer, play, reading
teach.note: Ask pupils how many hours they spend on screens; this is private, so use a show of fingers (0-1, 2-3, more). Discuss balance, not shame. Create a class ‘balance wheel’ with sections: learning, family, worship, play, rest, screens. Emphasise that balance is a Muslim virtue: moderation in everything.

practice: Sort into everyday or sometimes: (a) apple (b) fizzy drink (c) water (d) crisps (e) vegetables.
Fill in: ‘I need about ___ hours of sleep because…’
Why is it better to stop screens before bedtime?
independent: Design a healthy day plan: breakfast, school, exercise, family time, prayer, screens, bedtime. Add times.
Write three goals for staying healthy this week.
Draw a balance wheel with six parts and add one activity to each.
exit: Why do we need balance in how we use our time?
lessons.homework: Choose one goal from your plan and try it every day this week. Tick a chart each day.
lessons.send: SEND: provide picture-based plans and a visual timetable. EAL: key words with pictures. Stretch: research one healthy food from different cultures and share why it is healthy.
